staged_description.description_short: Government Speech Ban - 'Hit List of Forbidden Words' Implementation
staged_description.description_medium: NPR reported in April 2025 that climate- and environment-related terms, including “climate crisis” and “environmental justice,” were disappearing from some federal websites and documents. Researchers at federally funded institutions said they were advised to avoid phrases such as “climate change” and “biodiversity” in grant language. The White House denied creating a banned-word list, saying agencies interpreted executive orders.
staged_description.description_long: Donald Trump implemented Project 2025's explicit censorship program by banning hundreds of words and concepts from federal documents, creating what PEN America called a 'hit list of forbidden terms' that includes 'diversity,' 'gender,' 'reproductive health,' 'climate change,' 'environmental justice,' and 'any other term used to deprive Americans of their First Amendment rights.' The systematic word elimination represented unprecedented government censorship, with Heritage Foundation President Kevin Roberts directing that banned terms be 'deleted from every federal rule, agency regulation, contract, grant, regulation, and piece of legislation that exists.' Federal agencies removed climate change information from over 200 government websites while scientists receiving federal funding were told to avoid terms like 'climate change,' 'sustainable,' 'sustainability,' and even 'biodiversity' because it contains the word 'diversity.' The language purge extended beyond policy documents to include educational materials and public communications, with government employees reporting they 'can't speak the way that we normally would' due to fear of job loss or funding cuts. Environmental researchers confirmed being advised to avoid basic scientific terminology, with one noting 'we've just had cold water thrown on every single topic that involves humans and the environment.' The forbidden word list was explicitly described as non-final, with Project 2025 architects planning to 'expand their list of censored terms in the future,' creating an Orwellian system where government language must conform to conservative ideology rather than scientific accuracy or objective communication.

The educational apartheid created what civil rights organizations called return to pre-Brown era segregation through 'blueprint for the return of separate and unequal schools' that eliminated federal protections against discriminatory resource allocation while enabling racial and economic sorting through voucher systems designed to benefit privileged families. The school resegregation represented Project 2025's vision of education based on family wealth and racial preference rather than equal opportunity, transforming public education from system serving all students into mechanism that perpetuated inequality while using federal resources to subsidize private exclusion rather than public integration and educational equity.

staged_description.description_long: In June 2016, while Judge Gonzalo Curiel was overseeing class-action lawsuits brought by former students against Trump University, Donald Trump argued that Curiel could not judge the cases fairly because of his Mexican heritage. Curiel was born in Indiana to parents from Mexico. Trump linked the judge’s background to his own proposal to build a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border, calling it an “inherent conflict” and describing Curiel as Mexican despite the judge’s U.S. birthplace. In a CNN interview with Jake Tapper, Trump maintained that the judge’s heritage was relevant to whether he could rule impartially and rejected Tapper’s suggestion that disqualifying a judge on that basis was racist. The Washington Post reported that Trump had repeatedly made the argument as he challenged Curiel’s rulings in the Trump University litigation. The dispute drew criticism from legal experts and Republican leaders, who said ethnicity was not a legitimate basis to question a judge’s impartiality. The episode concerned the candidate’s public pressure on a judge in a case in which he was personally involved; the report does not establish that Curiel’s rulings were biased or that the court accepted Trump’s argument.

The charges were allegations presented by prosecutors and had to be tested in court; the grand jury’s decision to indict was not a finding that the defendants were guilty.

It rescinded guidance that treated book removals as potential civil rights violations and eliminated the book-ban coordinator position. The department also dismissed six additional allegations and annulled a settlement with Georgia’s Forsyth County School District. The combination changed the signals schools received about both removing books and teaching contested subjects. The order did not mean that schools had already lost funding, and the department’s decisions did not establish that every complaint was valid. The episode shows a shift in federal oversight during a period of widespread book challenges, with the practical effects depending on how districts and the government applied the new policies.

staged_description.title: Marko Elez Given Admin Write-Access to $5.4T Federal Payment System
staged_description.description_short: Marko Elez Given Admin Write-Access to $5.4T Federal Payment System
staged_description.description_medium: On February 1, 2025, Treasury gave DOGE staffer Marko Elez read and write access to two Bureau of the Fiscal Service payment systems. Those systems processed $5.45 trillion in federal payments in fiscal year 2024. Although officials publicly described access as read-only, later Treasury filings said write permission had been granted by mistake and was not used to alter the payment database.
staged_description.description_long: On February 1, 2025, the day after Treasury career official David Lebryk was placed on administrative leave for resisting DOGE, 25-year-old Marko Elez — a former SpaceX and X employee with no government or finance experience — was granted read and write access to the Bureau of the Fiscal Service's Payment Automation Manager (PAM) and Secure Payment System (SPS). These two systems processed $5.45 trillion in federal payments in fiscal year 2024, including Social Security checks, tax refunds, veterans' pay, and federal salaries. White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent repeatedly told Congress and the press that DOGE's access was read-only. Treasury officials actually altered internal records to indicate Elez no longer had write access before senior IT staff stated it was rescinded. Reporting by Wired and Talking Points Memo confirmed Elez had already made extensive changes to the code base for the payment systems. His write access was not revoked until February 5, the day a federal judge issued a temporary restraining order. Five former Treasury Secretaries warned in a New York Times op-ed that DOGE had put America's payments system and the highly sensitive data within it to the risk of exposure, potentially to our adversaries.

staged_description.title: Chanthila Souvannarath Deported to Laos Despite Federal Court Order and Citizenship Claim
staged_description.description_short: Chanthila Souvannarath Deported to Laos Despite Federal Court Order and Citizenship Claim
staged_description.description_medium: ICE deported Chanthila Souvannarath to Laos in late October 2025 after a federal judge ordered that he remain in the United States while his substantial citizenship claim was considered. Souvannarath, a longtime Alabama resident born in a refugee camp in Thailand, had been detained at the Louisiana State Penitentiary at Angola. His attorneys argued that his early lawful permanent residence supported a path to citizenship. The ACLU of Louisiana said the deportation defied the court order and separated a family.
staged_description.description_long: In late October 2025, ICE deported Chanthila Souvannarath, a 44-year-old father who had lived in Alabama for most of his life, to Laos — in direct defiance of a federal court order. US District Judge Shelly Dick had ordered ICE the previous week to keep Souvannarath in the United States while he presented what she described as a substantial claim of U.S. citizenship. Souvannarath was born in a refugee camp in Thailand but had been granted lawful permanent residence before his first birthday after his family fled to the United States. His attorneys argued this created a viable path to citizenship. After Judge Dick issued the restraining order, ICE deported him anyway. The ACLU of Louisiana, which represented Souvannarath, called the deportation a stunning violation of a federal court order, stating: ICE just ignored a federal court order and tore yet another family apart. Prior to his deportation, Souvannarath had been detained at a newly opened ICE facility at the Louisiana State Penitentiary at Angola — a maximum-security prison more commonly known for housing convicted felons serving life sentences, now repurposed as an ICE detention facility. His case was part of a broader pattern of the Trump administration defying judicial orders in immigration cases, beginning with the March 15, 2025 CECOT deportations conducted despite a court restraining order.

Former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci warned: Now, anyone globally can effectively deposit money into the bank account of the President of the United States with just a few clicks. Every favor — be it geopolitical, corporate, or personal — is now openly for sale. By mid-2025, Trump's 2026 financial disclosure revealed CIC Digital had taken in over $600 million from meme coin sales, while retail investors bore catastrophic losses as the coins collapsed more than two-thirds from peak.

staged_description.description_short: EPA Slashes 23% of Workforce, Shuts Down Science Office
staged_description.description_medium: On July 18, 2025, the EPA announced a planned reduction from 16,155 employees to 12,448, or about 23 percent, alongside a reorganization of its Office of Research and Development. The agency projected $748.8 million in savings. The plan raised concerns about the capacity for environmental research and enforcement, though the agency said scientific functions and many staff would be redistributed rather than simply eliminated.
staged_description.description_long:
The Environmental Protection Agency announced a major workforce reduction and reorganization on July 18, 2025. Its plan would reduce staffing from 16,155 to 12,448 employees, approximately 23 percent, and projected $748.8 million in savings. The Office of Research and Development was to be reorganized, not simply erased: EPA's announcement said its functions and many scientific staff would be redistributed across the agency. That distinction matters when describing the scale and nature of the change.

The restructuring nevertheless raised questions about how the agency would maintain independent research and carry out pollution enforcement, Superfund work, and water-protection responsibilities with fewer employees and a changed science structure. Environmental justice staff had also been affected by earlier workforce actions, according to the supplied record. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin presented the plan as an efficiency effort; critics warned that reduced capacity could weaken oversight and the scientific basis for regulation. The available figures describe a planned reorganization and projected savings, not proof that every announced reduction had already occurred or that every scientific position was eliminated. Its consequences would depend on how the agency redistributed expertise and handled its remaining statutory work.

The committee also found that the IRS had not performed the mandatory annual audits of Trump’s returns during his first two years in office; the agency began the process after House Democrats asked about it in 2019.

The disclosure created a public record of Trump’s reported income, deductions, losses, and foreign bank accounts while he was president. It also exposed a gap in the IRS’s oversight of a sitting president, whose returns were subject to annual review. The returns did not settle every question about Trump’s finances, but they allowed Congress and the public to examine information he had fought to keep private. The case raised broader issues of financial transparency and whether existing audit rules were being applied as required.
